1 pm - 5 pm Met Opera in HD: Così fan tutte (Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

This vibrant production sets the satirical comedy of fickle young love at a boardwalk amusement park.

Phelim McDermott's "colorful, inventive" (The New York Times) staging, inspired by Coney Island in the 1950s, sets the uproarious story at a boardwalk amusement park, where the two pairs of lovers at the heart of the tale find themselves on one emotional—and literal—thrill ride after another. Soprano Federica Lombardi and mezzo-soprano Samantha Hankey sing Fiordiligi and Dorabella, opposite tenor Duke Kim and baritone Andrey Zhilikhovsky as Ferrando and Guglielmo. Bass-baritone Gerald Finley reprises his portrayal of the cynical Don Alfonso, with soprano Ana María Martínez as the witty maid Despina.

Get more info and tickets here.

4:00 pm - 5:15 pm Underland (with writer Robert Macfarlane in person) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Based on Robert Macfarlane's bestseller, this hypnotic documentary follows three "astronauts of the underworld" on their journey below the surface of the earth.

Beginning in the shallow soil beneath an ancient ash tree, we travel into sacred ancient caves, flooded storm drains and deep underground laboratories designed to unravel the universe's mysteries. Narrated by Sandra Hüller with poetic sensitivity, the film presents a groundbreaking perspective on our relationship with the earth beneath our feet—a realm that most associate only with darkness and fear but that holds wonder and knowledge for those courageous enough to explore. 

Produced by Darren Aronofsky, Underland offers a rare documentary experience that serves simultaneously as visual splendor, an environmental statement and a philosophical inquiry. This film challenges perceptions and expands understanding of our planet's hidden dimensions, delivering beauty, science and wonder in equal measure, resulting in a profound reevaluation of the ground beneath our feet.

Discussion follows with writer Robert Macfarlane

Co-sponsored by the Department of Environmental Studies and the Department of Anthropology. Please also join us for Robert Macfarlane's writer's talk on Oct 5 in Top of the Hop.

Get more info and tickets here.

Sep 16 – Nov 14, 2026 a place visited only in dreams Linda Roesch Visual Arts Gallery and Gallery 3, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Opening reception Friday, September 25, 5-7 PM. On view September 16-November 14 | The Linda Roesch Visual Arts Gallery and Gallery 3

A Place Visited Only in Dreams brings together 35 artists who are each interested in exploring the shifting terrain of the subconscious, where logic dissolves and imagination reigns. Rooted in the legacy of Surrealism, this exhibition is composed of works that construct alternate realities—worlds shaped by dream imagery, memory fragments, intuition, and the irrational. Here, narratives unfold beyond the boundaries of waking life, where objects may float, figures transform, scale collapses, and time behaves unpredictably.

Surrealism has long offered a visual language for expressing what cannot be spoken directly: desire, fear, wonder, longing, and the strange poetry of the mind at rest. In this exhibition, you'll find artworks that embrace unexpected juxtapositions, uncanny atmospheres, and illogical pairings that provoke both unease and fascination. Whether playful or haunting, meditative or disruptive, these works invite viewers to step into spaces that feel familiar yet impossible— places visited only in dreams.

Step beyond waking reality. Enter the dream.

Exhibiting artists: Amy Abeyta, Jenna Marie Alderiso, Lucas Barrett, Kalli Bechtold, Fiorella Buck, Annabelle Cone, Annemarie Curlin, Elizabeth D'Amico, Thia Daniels, Samantha Eckert, Richard Fedorchak, Stephanie Gordon, Laura Graveline, Matthew Greenway, Naomi Hartov, Bruce Hasse, Marria Khan, Ed Kimball, Stephany Komen Hasse, Maggie mayfly Kundtz Joseph, Susan Maerlender, Emma Mehegan, Carl Mehrbach, Michaela Meyer, Jennifer Rickards, Lara Ronan, Kerin Rose, Cynthia Ross, Ann Saunderson, Tom Sennett, Nancy Sepe, Reinhart Sonnenburg, Richard Stamelman, Rio Del Sol Vasquez-Billin, Cathy Vincevic

Sep 25 – Nov 14, 2026 Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee | Jason Pappas Main Gallery- AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Opening Reception Friday, September 25, 5-7 PM through November 14, 2026 | Linda Bryan; Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan; Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee; Jason Pappas (Linda Bryan; Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan on separate event page)

We are pleased to present four distinct but interconnected exhibitions that explore how we understand the past, navigate uncertainty, and carry traces of history into the present. Through photography, painting, drawing, assemblage, and sculpture, the artists consider memory, place, family, perception, and the enduring relationship between people and the materials and environments they inhabit.

E. N. Wennberg Gallery: Mapping Uncertainty features Andrea Kantrowitz and Jeesoo Lee, whose practices meet in their exploration of perception, transformation, displacement, and change. Kantrowitz’s expansive sumi ink landscapes, informed by the Hudson Valley and Chinese literati painting, evoke environments that are simultaneously familiar and elusive. Lee’s delicate assemblages of translucent paper and thread occupy a more intimate scale, reflecting experiences of hesitation, displacement, belonging, and connection. Although their approaches differ, both artists embrace uncertainty not as an obstacle to overcome, but as a productive condition in which new possibilities can emerge. Their shared artistic history, dating back to a 2009 exhibition, gives the current presentation an added sense of continuity and renewed dialogue.

Rebecca Lawrence Gallery Entry: Jason Pappas’s Relics from the Human Age turns to the physical landscape as a record of human history and intention. Working with trees that fell on his Vermont property, Pappas discovered not only a source of material but traces of the people who had shaped the land before him. The property’s gardens, plantings, workshop, and remnants of earlier woodworking reveal layers of labor, foresight, and care extending across generations. By transforming salvaged wood into new works, Pappas carries these histories forward without attempting to recreate them exactly. The resulting objects function simultaneously as sculpture, artifact, and continuation—reminders that actions taken by one generation can shape lives far into the future.

Taken together, these four exhibitions offer a meditation on what remains: the photograph that outlives the memory, the painting that transforms recollection, the landscape that shifts beneath our feet, and the material traces left behind by those who came before us. Each exhibition approaches the past differently, yet all four ask us to consider how histories are preserved, altered, inherited, and reimagined. Across these varied practices, the artists suggest that looking backward is not simply an act of remembrance, can be a way of understanding where we are now and imagining what we might carry forward.

Sep 25 – Nov 14, 2026 Linda Bryan | Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan Main Gallery- AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Opening Reception Friday, September 25, 5-7 PM through November 14, 2026 | Linda Bryan; Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan; Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee; Jason Pappas (Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee; Jason Pappas on separate event page)

We are pleased to present four distinct but interconnected exhibitions that explore how we understand the past, navigate uncertainty, and carry traces of history into the present. Through photography, painting, drawing, assemblage, and sculpture, the artists consider memory, place, family, perception, and the enduring relationship between people and the materials and environments they inhabit.

Elizabeth Rowland Mayor Gallery: In Falling Leaves, Linda Bryan examines the fragile relationship between memory and evidence. Drawing from family photographs, documents, objects, and ephemera, Bryan considers how the stories we inherit—and the stories we tell ourselves—can shift over time. A childhood photograph, a handwritten note, and other fragments of family history become points of departure for questioning what is remembered, what is forgotten, and what remains when direct access to the past begins to disappear. The resulting works form an intimate and incomplete family archive, suggesting that personal history is not fixed, but continually reconstructed from the fragments that survive.

Clifford B. West Gallery: Past Forward brings together the work of Jim Jordan and Rachel Jordan in a dialogue between memory, observation, history, and abstraction. Jim Jordan draws on recollections of childhood and adolescence in the 1940s and 1950s, transforming those memories through the visual language of Modernism. Rachel Jordan approaches the still life through a contemporary lens, engaging with a rich history of artistic traditions while exploring the relationships among objects, space, form, and perception. Together, their paintings demonstrate how the past can be revisited and transformed rather than simply remembered, allowing personal experience, art history, and abstraction to generate new ways of seeing the present.

Taken together, these four exhibitions offer a meditation on what remains: the photograph that outlives the memory, the painting that transforms recollection, the landscape that shifts beneath our feet, and the material traces left behind by those who came before us. Each exhibition approaches the past differently, yet all four ask us to consider how histories are preserved, altered, inherited, and reimagined. Across these varied practices, the artists suggest that looking backward is not simply an act of remembrance, can be a way of understanding where we are now and imagining what we might carry forward.

Sessions start 12:00 am

Open Call to AVA Members! AVA Members’ Holiday Exhibition and Sale | No entry fee! You must be an active AVA Member to Participate. The sales commission for this year’s holiday exhibition will be 70% to artists and 30% AVA.

Important Dates:

Entry Deadline: Monday, November 2

Delivery: Thursday, November 19, 10-4 pm.

Pick up: Tuesday, January 5 and Wednesday, January 6, 10-4 pm.

This year AVA is hosting a Makers Market alongside the exhibition. The exhibition will be featured in the Linda Roesch Visual Arts Gallery, the Rebecca Lawrence Gallery Entry, and the Clifford B. West Gallery. The Makers Market will be featured in the E.N. Wennberg Gallery and the Elizabeth Rowland Mayor Gallery.

For this year’s Holiday Exhibition and Sale, we would like to focus on small works both in 2D wall hung works and ceramics, think gifts and pieces that are easy for folks to collect—both in size/scale and price.

For 2D there are 2 choices:

1. You may submit up to 4 pieces, each up to 12”.

OR,

2. If you have work over this scale, then 2 are permitted, each up to 24”.

You must wire these works as so: the wire must be installed at the same position on each piece, at 3 inches below the top stretcher bar or frame. Works must align with these instructions.

We recommend that you price the 2D smalls (up to 12”) at $200 or under. For the (up to 24”) at $400 and under.

For ceramics there are 2 choices:

1. You may submit up to 8 pieces, under 12” each.

OR,

2. Or if you have larger works, 2 pieces up to 24”

Your local cemetery is a time capsule. Each headstone is plastered with clues about the deceased, those who once walked where you walk now. A simple step through the hallowed gates can bring you on an adventure to explore symbolism, workmanship, and local history. Join Erin E. Moulton as we learn the meaning behind cemetery iconography, abbreviations, epitaphs, and more.

3:30 pm - 5:00 pm Kimberlé Crenshaw | 10.5.26 Filene Auditorium, Moore Building

The Institute for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life in collaboration with the Department of African and African American Studies and The Susan and James Wright Center for the Study of Computation and Just Communities would like to invite you to the following event:

On Monday, October 5th, American legal scholar, Kimberlé Williams Crenshaw, who coined the term "intersectionality", will be speaking on campus about her recent book, BACKTALKER. This event will take place in Filene Auditorium at 3:30pm. This conversation will be led by Dr. Bria Paige, the 2025-2027 Thurgood Marshall Fellow in AAAS.

Kimberlé Williams Crenshaw is a pioneering scholar and writer on civil rights, Black feminist legal theory, and race, racism, and the law. She was a founder and has been a leader in the intellectual movement called critical race theory, and is also known for introducing and developing the concept of intersectionality. She is a Distinguished Professor of Law and the Promise Institute Chair in Human Rights at the University of California, Los Angeles; the Isidor and Seville Sulzbacher Professor of Law at Columbia Law School; and the cofounder and executive director of the African American Policy Forum. The author of the New York Times bestseller Backtalker: An American Memoir, she has appeared as a commentator on media outlets including MSNBC and NPR, and hosts the podcast Intersectionality Matters!


 

 

African and African-American Studies Program, History Department, Institute for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life, Philosophy Department, Rockefeller Center, Sociology Department, Wright Center

5 pm - 6 pm Lecture on Inequality, Discrimination, and Opportunity Room 003, Rockefeller Center

The Department of Economics is pleased to sponsor this lecture series to deepen Dartmouth students' understanding of the role of inequality, discrimination, and opportunity in society and to highlight how economics can increase our understanding of these phenomena and inform policy responses.

Regularization and Development. A Decade of Evidence from Colombia

Abstract:
Colombia stands as a pioneer in refugee policy. By granting a regularization status to more than two million Venezuelans, it has showcased the potential of a self-inclusion model in which refugees can work, move freely, and access public services as any other vulnerable population. This lecture summarizes a decade of research on what that model has meant for the economic, social, and political structures of host communities, and for the lives of migrants themselves, in both the short and the long run. It closes with two new studies, one tracing the medium run effects of regularization on migrant social capital, the other its public health externalities.

Sandra V. Rozo is a Senior Economist in the Development Research Group at the World Bank, Faculty Affiliate at UC Berkeley’s CEGA and EGAP, Research Fellow at IZA, and Associate Editor of the Journal of Development Economics. Her research examines how forced displacement affects development and how we can support displaced populations and their hosting communities effectively. She co-founded major studies on forced migration, including VenRePs and the Syrian Refugee Life Study, and contributed to the World Development Report 2023. She is the recipient of the 2024 Juan Luis Londoño Award, awarded biennially to Colombians under 40 whose work has significantly improved welfare in Colombia. Her work spans Latin America, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Africa, including multiple randomized control trials.

Co-Sponsored with:  Sadie Alexander Association

5:00 pm - 6:30 pm The Robert F. Allabough 1934 Memorial History Lecture with A.K. Sandoval-Strausz Carson Hall L01
 

The Department of History welcomes guest scholar A. K. Sandoval-Strausz (Professor of History at Penn State University), to give the annual Robert F. Allabough 1934 Memorial Lecture for Fall 2026:

"Latinos in Rust Belt Pennsylvania: and the Origins of Trumpist Politics"

In a study of shifting power struggles and early anti-immigrant campaigns in urban Pennsylvania, Professor Sandoval-Strausz presents Latino communities in the Rust Belt as key to understanding the momentous political realignment that is currently underway nationally: the rise of right-wing populism.

Sandoval-Strausz was born in New York City to immigrant parents. He teaches courses in Latino studies, urban history, spatial theory, sociability, and immigration. He is a National Endowment for the Humanities Public Scholar and a Distinguished Lecturer of the Organization of American Historians. His books have won multiple international history awards: Hotel: An American History (Yale University Press, 2007) and Barrio America: How Latino Immigrants Saved the American City (Basic Books, 2019). More at: https://history.la.psu.edu/directory/a-k-sandoval-strausz/.

5:30 pm - 7:00 pm Fall 2026 George Link Jr. Environmental Awareness Lecture Top of the Hop, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Join us on October 5th at 5:30pm in the Top of the Hop for our Fall 2026 George Link Jr. Environmental Awareness Lecture with bestselling author, Robert Macfarlane!
From the Elwha to the Klamath: on the lives, deaths and rights of rivers

A contemporary de-damming movement is sweeping Europe and the United States. Last year 542 dams were removed across 23 European countries, and 100 dams came down across 30 US states, reconnecting 4900 miles of waterway: more than in any previous year in history. New Hampshire is part of this shift, with dams coming down on the Cocheco, the Piscataquog and the Merrimack, among others. The de-damming movement has accelerated in tandem with, and often in partnership with, the Rights of Nature movement, which argues for a categorical shift in perception and treatment (legal, structural and cultural-imaginative) of ecosystems from resource to relative, object to fellow subject and use value to intrinsic value –– and proposes recognizing rivers always-already as the bearers of fundamental rights.

This 2026 George Link Jr Environmental Awareness Lecture by the British writer Robert Macfarlane will explore what flows from the recognition of rivers as having lives, deaths and rights. By means of story and reportage as well as history, it will traces some of the complex, contested histories of de-damming and river-rights movements, from the Elwha and Klamath rivers in the Pacific Northwest, the Mutehekau Shipu (Magpie River) in Nitassinan (north-east Québec), the Río Los Cedros in Ecuador, and the resurgent 'river-guardianship' movement in England. It will also argue for the vital roles of storytelling, music and art (or what Arne Naess called 'beautiful acts') in inspiring river-activism and, by extension, wider global currents of change.

This event is sponsored by the Hopkins Center for the Arts at Dartmouth, the Department of Environmental Studies, and the Department of Anthropology.

https://envs.dartmouth.edu/news/2026/10/fall-2026-george-link-jr-environmental-awareness-lecture

2:30 pm - 3:30 pm Space and Plasma Seminar - Zesen Huang, UCLA academic Wilder 202 and Zoom

Abstract: Near the Sun, Parker Solar Probe encounters large-amplitude Alfvénic fluctuations and abrupt magnetic-field reversals known as switchbacks. What three-dimensional wave structure could produce these one-dimensional spacecraft signatures? Building on our recent paper, I will introduce the Alfvénon: a numerical realization of a solitary Alfvén wave with an undisturbed far field, open magnetic-field-line topology, and nearly constant magnetic-field strength. A spacecraft crossing its curved field lines can record a switchback-like reversal, while direct ideal-MHD simulations show coherent propagation over the simulated interval. This provides a testable physical picture of switchbacks without claiming that one structure explains every event or remains stable indefinitely. I will also discuss how AI assisted the discovery: exploratory work with Claude helped us formulate an alternating-projection method for constructing the constrained magnetic geometry and aided code debugging. We independently implemented and tested the method, checked its physical constraints, ran the simulations, and interpreted the results. Together, these results mark a fundamental advance in Alfvén-wave physics and open a new way to study nonlinear magnetic structures across the solar wind and other magnetized plasma environments.

Hosted by Assistant Professor Muni Zhou 

Zoom Link: https://dartmouth.zoom.us/j/99960465228?

5 pm - 6 pm AI, Cybersecurity, and National Defense Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

Artificial intelligence, cyber operations, and emerging technologies are rapidly changing the landscape of U.S. national security, transforming how threats are detected, decisions are made, and conflicts are fought. In conversation with Government Professor Daryl Press, Emily Harding will discuss how these technologies are reshaping intelligence work and national defense. Drawing on her experience at the CIA, the National Security Council, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and CSIS, Harding will examine how policymakers and intelligence professionals are adapting to an era of faster information, more complex threats, and intensifying strategic competition.

This event will be recorded. Livestream registration (webinar): here | In-person tickets: here

Emily Harding serves as vice president of the Defense and Security Department and director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, where she leads work on the future of intelligence, emerging technology, and national security policy. Previously, she served as deputy staff director of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, where she led the committee’s bipartisan investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. She spent much of her earlier career at the Central Intelligence Agency, leading analysts and analytic programs through major crises, including the attempted Islamic State takeover in Iraq. Harding also served at the National Security Council as director for Iran and later helped run the first Office of the Director of National Intelligence-led presidential transition, briefing the incoming administration. She is an adjunct lecturer at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, and her analysis has appeared in the Wall Street Journal, BBC, NPR, Bloomberg, and other outlets. She holds a master’s degree from Harvard Kennedy School and a B.A. from the University of Virginia.

Co-sponsored by the Alexander Hamilton Society and the Davidson Institute for Global Security at the Dickey Center.

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm Artist Talk: Janet Echelman (Noli Timere) Hood Auditorium

Sculptor Janet Echelman talks about her practice of melding art, engineering, and climate data.

Janet Echelman sculpts at the scale of buildings and city blocks, creating large-scale, fluid installations that merge art, architecture and engineering to anchor public spaces across five continents. Her work transforms with wind and light, inviting viewers into immersive experiences rather than static observation. Echelman uses unlikely materials—from atomized water particles to fiber stronger than steel—blending traditional craft with advanced computational design. Echelman's unconventional path includes five years living in a Balinese village, graduate studies in both painting and psychology, and teaching at MIT, Harvard and Princeton. Oprah ranked Echelman's work #1 on her List of 50 Things That Make You Say Wow!, and she received the Guggenheim Fellowship and the Smithsonian American Ingenuity Award in Visual Arts, honoring "the greatest innovators in America today."

There will be a book signing after the talk. Books will be available for sale.

3:30 pm - 4:15 pm Guided Relaxation with iRest yoga Nidra, and Journaling Rollins Chapel

All dates: Oct 7, Oct 14, Oct 21, Oct 28, Nov 4

The SWC is excited to bring you a mid-week restorative practice* with to-go healthy snacks and journals!

This experiential learning opportunity will take place every Wednesday from 3:30 to 4:15pm. Each session will look something like this: 
- Setup mats and settle into our spaces (5- minutes) 
- Guided yoga nidra (25- minutes)
- Prompted free-write in provided journals (6 minutes)
- Debrief and optional sharing time (6 min) 
- Ending session and putting away mats, journals (3 minutes) 

*mats will be provided

What is Yoga Nidra?

Yoga nidra is a type of meditation practice originating from ancient India, commonly known as "yogic sleep" or "dynamic sleep." It is a contemplative practice that involves following guided prompts while lying in a comfortable position through various stages of relaxation, breathing exercises, and visualization.

This practice aims to induce a state of deep relaxation and meditation, similar to the liminal state between waking and sleeping. This state can provide numerous physical, emotional, and mental benefits, such as reducing stress and anxiety, improving sleep, enhancing creativity, and promoting overall well-being. In this state, you may experience a sense of timelessness, expansiveness, and interconnectedness.

12:15 pm - 1:00 pm Research Talk– Chris Sollars: The Neighbors 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center

Mankin's research on climate variability and change is motivated by the risks global warming poses to ecosystems and people. Using observations alongside empirical and process-based models, his efforts are prospective—focused constraining uncertainties in future climate impacts—and retrospective—attributing the climate impacts that have already occured. He is committed to ensuring that climate data are a public good and his hope is that his science can help inform climate adaptation and decision-making. In his previous career, Dr. Mankin worked overseas as an intelligence officer.

PhD candidate in Ecology, Evolution, Environment, & Society, Joseph Savage works with Jonathan Winter in the Geography Department as a part of the Applied Hydroclimatology Group to study tick populations and the impact of climate change. Savage's interests center on disease and community ecology, and use theoretical techniques to study these complex systems. Their current research focuses on understanding and forecasting how climate and landscape changes are driving the population dynamics and pathogen prevalence of Ixodes scapularis--the blacklegged tick--which is responsible for spreading Lyme disease in the Northeast.

This programming accompanies a faculty exhibition by Associate Professor of Studio Art Chris Sollars, The Neighbors, a new body of work inspired by coexistence and inquiry.

Set in rural Vermont, The Neighbors is a multimedia video installation about the non-human inhabitants of the lands around the artist’s home. After over two decades living in San Francisco, California, Sollars moved to Vermont in the fall of 2024. To get to know his new home and neighbors, he has spent the past two years interacting with his surroundings through slow listening and observation, learning them spatially and temporally.  This intentional gathering of information has taken the form of diaristic snapshots taken throughout the seasons, field recordings, the collection of discarded nests and materials, and the placement of wildlife cameras in the open woodland edges of his home, which neighbors a land trust, a national forest, and the Appalachian Trail.

The Neighbors is on view from Sept. 15 – Nov. 8, 2026.

5:00pm Meet Lucy Stone: Enter the Antebellum World of the Abolition and Women's Rights Movements Gay Kimball Library 10 South Main Street Troy New Hampshire 03465

In this first-person interpretive program, Judith Black introduces American Lucy Stone, the first woman hired by the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society as a public speaker and the "Shining Star" of the Abolition and Women's Rights Movements. The presenter dispels well-worn platitudes about the antebellum North by interjecting historic and personal truths about these social reform movements. Her presentation also paints a dynamic and detailed picture of what it takes to change the world you are born into. Follow Lucy as she makes her case for tax resistance, her challenges to marriage laws and motherhood, and her pro-Emancipation response to the Civil War. Go with her to The American Equal Rights Association Convention in May 1869, where she eloquently supports the 15th Amendment, which gave African-American men the vote. 

This is an in person event. We will provide refreshments. This event is open to the public.

6:00pm Covered Bridges of New Hampshire - Past and Present Meredith Public Library 91 Main Street Meredith NH 03253

New Hampshire was once home to over 300 covered bridges. Today, there are over sixty authentic covered bridges in New Hampshire, forty-six of which are over a century old. These bridges exist solely because of the efforts of a small but powerful community that both recognized their significance and honored their tradition. Join author and photographer Kim Varney Chandler as she shares an overview of covered bridges in the Granite State, along with interesting facts she uncovered while researching her 2022 book, Covered Bridges of New Hampshire. Learn more about both existing and lost covered bridges in your area.

Our meeting room is accessible and parking is available at the back of the building off of High Street.

6:00pm The Connecticut: New England's Great River Claremont Claremont NH 03743

The largest river in New England rises in a small beaver pond near the Canadian border and flows over 400 miles through four states, falling 2,670 feet to the sea through America's only watershed-based national fish and wildlife refuge. Adair Mulligan leads an armchair tour of this great river in New Hampshire and Vermont, exploring its history and natural beauty through the seasons and among the communities that have sprung up along its banks. Next, the discussion will shift to how the river has influenced the lives of those who live there, and how they, in turn, have affected the river. Much more than a travelogue, this presentation explores the many issues involved in managing the health of this major river, and how citizens from all walks of life have created a vision for its future.

6:30pm Brewing in New Hampshire: An Informal History of Beer in the Granite State Oscar Foss Memorial Library 111 South Barnstead Road Barnstead NH 03225

Glenn Knoblock explores the fascinating history of New Hampshire's beer and ale brewing industry from Colonial days, when it was home- and tavern-based, to today's modern breweries and brew pubs. Unusual and rare photos and advertisements document this changing industry and the state's earliest brewers, including the renowned Frank Jones. A number of lesser-known brewers and breweries that operated in the state are also discussed, including the only brewery owned and operated by a woman before the modern era. Illustrations present evidence of society's changing attitudes towards beer and alcohol consumption over the years. Whether you're a beer connoisseur or a "tea-totaler", this lecture will be enjoyed by adults of all ages.

7 pm - 9 pm The Alabama Solution Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Inside one of the nation's deadliest prison systems, incarcerated men defy the odds to expose a cover-up in this Oscar-nominated documentary.

In 2019, filmmakers Andrew Jarecki and Charlotte Kaufman visit an Alabama prison to film a revival meeting. Off camera, incarcerated men whisper a message: terrible things are going on here and being kept secret. This sparks an immersive six-year investigation to discover the reality behind the walls of one of the nation's deadliest prison systems.

Composed primarily of contraband cell phone footage taken by incarcerated men at Easterling and other facilities across the state, The Alabama Solution exposes the inhumane conditions, systemic injustice and brutal treatment of those behind bars in the Alabama prison system, told through their own voices and their own stories. The film expertly weaves the pressing issues of prison privatization, inmate slave labor, abuse of power, government corruption and extreme violence together to help audiences on the outside get a real sense of the abhorrent conditions of our fellow human beings. 

Programmed in collaboration with the Dartmouth Prison Justice Initiative. Discussion follows.

 

This event is free but registration is required.

 

Get more info and register here.

7:00 pm - 8:30 pm This Book is Full of Holes: yasser elhariry book launch Still North Book Store

For millennia, the figure of the hole stood as the cornerstone for idioms and expressions that denote emptiness, lack, absences, and voids. A hole demands to be filled. This Book Is Full of Holes challenges these hollow associations, offering instead a range of provocative religious, sociosexual, philosophical, and scientific discourses. Drawing on a wide range of literary and cultural objects, yasser elhariry brings
disparate discursive spheres into conversation, nimbly juxtaposing the holey relationships between ancient Hebrew riddles and Hollywood space movies, ’90s grunge and Black astrophysics, Swiss cheese and philosophy, sacred ritual and post-colonial feminism. Satirical, dead serious, and deeply personal, elhariry’s treatise reveals why holes maintain a persistent hold on the imagination. His stylish analysis reveals their overlooked racialized, gendered, homophobic, and corporeal histories. Holes have been weaponized. This Book Is Full of Holes disarms.

11:00 am Shaker Herb Garden Tour Enfield Shaker Museum Garden

All dates: Oct 9, Oct 16, Oct 23, Oct 30

Weekly Shaker Herb Garden Tour

with Herbalist Happy Griffiths

Fridays at 11 am, meet by the rose bushes in the garden

Join renowned herbalist and founder of the Enfield Shaker Museum Herb Garden, Happy Griffiths, for a guided tour through one of the Museum’s most beloved living exhibits.

Discover the fascinating history of the Shakers’ herb-growing traditions as you explore beds of culinary, medicinal, aromatic, and dye plants. Along the way, Happy will share stories of how these herbs were cultivated and used by the Enfield Shakers, as well as their practical uses in today’s gardens and homes.

With decades of experience as an herbalist, educator, and the visionary behind the Museum’s herb garden, Happy brings each tour to life with engaging insights and a deep appreciation for the connections between people, plants, and history. The Museum’s herb garden features many of the same plants that were grown by the Shakers as part of their thriving herb and medicine enterprise.

Fridays at 11:00 a.m.

Tours are free with Museum admission and are open to visitors of all ages. Whether you’re an avid gardener, curious about herbal traditions, or simply looking for a beautiful way to experience the Museum grounds, this tour offers a unique opportunity to explore the living legacy of the Enfield Shakers.

What to Expect

Tours last approximately one hour and take place rain or shine, except in the case of thunder or lightning. Much of the tour is outdoors in full sun, so we recommend dressing for the weather, wearing comfortable walking shoes, and bringing water, sunscreen, or rain gear as needed.

The herb garden features maintained paths, but visitors should expect some uneven terrain. Benches are available in both sunny and shaded areas throughout the garden for those who would like to sit during the tour.

Visitors are encouraged to engage all of their senses. You’ll have opportunities to see, smell, and ~when invited by your guide~ even taste selected herbs. To help preserve the garden and support the Museum’s educational mission, we ask that visitors do not pick plants or harvest herbs during the tour.

Oct 9 Oct 23 Oct 30 Nov 6
2 pm - 3 pm MS Thesis Defense: Ryan Proulx academic Rm 007, ECSC (Design Loft)

Abstract: Countries such as the Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia face cycles of conflict, political instability, low electrification rates, and the impacts of climate change. Renewable energy-driven electrification is often considered an important way to mitigate these challenges. However, designing and planning green electrification initiatives in fragile states requires making complex planning decisions. We present a consensus-building framework and methodology to guide hybrid renewable energy systems planning in fragile states. Our study develops an iterative approach to Majority Judgment (MJ) for planning energy systems for United Nations (UN) compounds and the surrounding local community. The case study structure reflects a typical mini-grid demand profile involving an anchor client and a neighboring community.

We gather institutional data from 17 experts in African energy transition initiatives from groups including the African Development Bank, the UN Department of Operational Support, and the International Renewable Energy Agency. We elicit institutional knowledge via three institutional data collection channels: (1) organizations’ priorities when evaluating mini-grid projects, (2) organizations’ ranking of individual objectives, and (3) organizations’ evaluations of a set of Pareto-optimal mini-grid designs.

Leveraging these data, we implement three methods to process the institutional knowledge: (1) fitting utility functions to LLM (Large Language Model)-produced grades based on channel 1 institutional data, (2) generating utility functions based on channel 2 institutional data, and (3) fitting utility functions to stakeholder grades based on channel 3 institutional data. We compute the optimality gaps across all input methods in a 2-dimensional case (examining upfront cost and diesel consumption) and a 4-dimensional case (additionally examining community coverage, and system reliability). We find that low-diesel, high-community-coverage mini-grid designs, with reliability marginally below 100%, provide the best compromise in most cases across all input classes. Reliability proves to be a key lever that can significantly facilitate or hinder consensus-building. Overall, our results demonstrate that the proposed mechanism provides high-quality, near-optimal solutions under a limited-information setting, enabling deep insights into the practical nature of consensus solutions. Ultimately, our approach provides a blueprint backed by real stakeholder inputs and site-specific energy transition datasets with potential to accelerate electricity access in fragile states.

Thesis Committee: (Chair) Vikrant Vaze, Steven Peterson, Geoffrey Parker, Erin Mayfield, and Victoria Holt (Dickey Center for International Understanding)

2:15 pm - 3:15 pm Physics and Astronomy Colloquium - Professor Marla Geha, Yale academic Wilder 104 and Zoom

Abstract: The Milky Way's satellite galaxies have been used to constrain dark matter properties and explore the faintest threshold of galaxy formation.   These population-level studies rely on properties derived from heterogeneous spectroscopic analyses. Systematic differences between data reduction pipelines and membership criteria can masquerade as astrophysical signals, or obscure real trends.    I present the largest self-consistent sample of spectroscopically-derived quantities for Milky Way and M31 satellite galaxies based on a homogeneous re-analysis of individual stars observed with the Keck/DEIMOS spectrograph.    I demonstrate improved precision in the internal velocity dispersions over literature values, directly translating into improved constraints on their dark matter content and dark matter particle properties.  I then explore key relationships including the mass-metallicity and stellar mass-halo mass relationships.

Hosted by Assistant Professor Burçin Mutlu-Pakdil

Zoom Webinar Link: https://dartmouth.zoom.us/j/91888702369?pwd=aUlaVEFYNGZHNlZWL0R3cEVWQXg4UT09

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm High-Throughput Computational Microscopy with Dynamic Samples Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 937 4316 0035
Passcode: 411385

Computational imaging jointly designs hardware and algorithms to push beyond the classical limits of imaging, enabling measurement of new quantities (eg 3D, phase, and super-resolution) with simple, inexpensive hardware. In this talk, I show recent advances that push both spatial and temporal throughput for 2D and 3D fluorescence microscopy. First, I will describe a diffractive, multiplexed microscope that uses engineered point spread functions and a multi-sensor array to achieve gigapixel-scale imaging at video rates, enabling micrometer-resolution imaging over centimeter-scale fields of view for dynamic biological systems. Second, I will introduce a neural space-time model that jointly reconstructs images and motion from sequential measurements, eliminating motion artifacts while recovering sample dynamics without training data or priors. Together, these approaches illustrate a shift from static imaging toward high-throughput, dynamic measurement, opening new opportunities for observing complex biological processes across scales.

Hosted by Professor Irene Georgakoudi

5:30 pm - 6:30 pm Yang Yi: A Celebration of Classical Chinese Poetry and Music Filene Auditorium, Moore Building

Yang Yi is a renowned Chinese musician and educator. In the 1990s, he emerged as a pioneer of contemporary folk music in China and was hailed as “China’s Bob Dylan.” Over the past two decades, he and his team have developed an innovative educational approach that brings together traditional poetry chanting, calligraphy, painting, and classical Chinese music. A number of their students have gone on to become accomplished artists of a younger generation.

In this performance at Dartmouth, Yang will play traditional Chinese instruments and perform works by some of China’s greatest classical poets—including Tao Qian and Su Shi—as well as ancient yuefu (Music Bureau) ballads through traditional chanting in Mandarin, Cantonese, and Hakka.

The event is free and open to the public. English translations of the poems will be provided.
Sponsored by the Leslie Center for the Humanities "Innovative Chinese Curriculum Project" Venn Vision Grant

7:00 pm - 9:15 pm El Norte (DFS: Myths Revisited) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Gregory Nava's dramatic 1983 masterpiece weaves in elements of Aztec and Mayan mythology with a quest for the American dream.

After their family is killed in a union-busting government massacre, indigenous Mayan siblings Enrique and Rosa decide to flee Guatemala and embark on a perilous journey to America— "El Norte"—in search of a better life. Facing danger and persecution on every step of the way, their love and resolve eventually bring them to shimmery Los Angeles, which soon proves to be gilded rather than gold.

A tour de force of independent filmmaking, Pava expertly weaves Aztec and Mayan mythology with the modern American Dream, blending magical realism with poignant social commentary as he captures the realities of the modern immigrant experience.

Programmed in collaboration with Professor Gerd Gemunden's class on Migration Stories

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited"

7:30 pm - 8:30 pm Noli Timere Moore Theater, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Witness a gravity-defying world that challenges us to "be not afraid."

Director & Choreographer: Rebecca Lazier
Visual Artist: Janet Echelman
Composer: Jorane

A vast web sets the stage for a breathtaking aerial experience that reflects the interdependence among humans and our environment. Conceived by Guggenheim Fellowship Award-winning choreographer Rebecca Lazier and large-scale fiber artist Janet Echelman, Noli Timere dissolves the boundary between choreography and sculpture, creating a shared system in which body and environment continuously transform one another. A special 4-week lecture series!

Join David Bisno for a spirited discussion of the complicated relationships between Iranians, Americans, and the English. What was the path by which American hubris, ineptitude, delusions, and catastrophic miscalculations led to the present situation? What part did oil, Communists, Israelis, shahs, and an Islamic God play in the story? We will unveil not a single error but a pattern of English greed and American inattentiveness, bureaucratic in-fighting, and a string of strategic blunders allowing unnecessary crises to become a historic rupture with worldwide repercussions. 

David Bisno, a retired ophthalmologist with degrees from Harvard, Dartmouth, and the Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis), has, for the past 33 years, developed and presented courses on a myriad of subjects for ILEAD/Osher and for other institutes for lifelong learning across this country and overseas. He is known for clear, fair, nuanced presentations of provocative, complicated topics, engaging his students with energy and enthusiasm. He looks forward to lively discussion.

10:00am Discovering New England Stone Walls Plaistow Public Library 85 Main Street Plaistow New Hampshire 03865

Why are we so fascinated with stone walls? Kevin Gardner, author of The Granite Kiss, explains how and why New England came to acquire its thousands of miles of stone walls, the ways that they and other dry stone structures were built, how their styles emerged and changed over time, and their significance to the famous New England landscape. Along the way, Kevin occupies himself building a miniature wall or walls on a tabletop, using tiny stones from a five-gallon bucket. 

Please join us at the Plaistow Public Library where we have the accessibility and parking onsite.

Add to Google Calendar
10:00am The History of Agriculture as Told by Barns Greenfield Historical society 828 Forest Road Greenfield, NH NH 03047

Barns can tell us a great deal about the history of agriculture in New Hampshire. In the colonial period, New Hampshire was a rural, agrarian state and small subsistence farms dotted the landscape. An important part of these farmsteads was the barn, which housed animals and stored crops. Early barns used traditional building methods and followed the English barn style, with a low pitched roof and doors under the eaves. As time went on, the farms expanded to accommodate changes in agriculture. This presentation will follow the progression of barn styles that evolved to handle the increased productivity required to meet the needs of a growing population and respond to changes in society caused by the railroad and the Industrial Revolution. John C. Porter, author of Preserving Old Barns: Preventing the Loss of a Valuable Resource, will demonstrate how these majestic barn structures represent Yankee ingenuity, hard work, and skilled craftsmanship, as well as providing a link to our past that adds to the state's scenic beauty. 

This will be an in-person program with a light lunch available. This program is being coordinated with the dedication of our new barn/carriage shed, honoring a fine former Greenfield resident, Carl Inglestrom, who spent his career in the field of agriculture. The venue will be at least partially outside, weather permitting.

12:00 pm Shaker Herb Garden Tour Enfield Shaker Museum Garden

All dates: Oct 10, Oct 17, Oct 24, Oct 31

Weekly Shaker Herb Garden Tour

with Museum Interpreter Lisa Torres

Saturdays at Noon, meet by the Great Stone Dwelling, outside the Gift Shop Entrance

Join Museum Interpreter Lisa Torres for a guided tour through the Enfield Shaker Museum Herb Garden, one of the Museum’s most beloved living exhibits.

Discover the fascinating history of the Shakers’ herb-growing traditions as you explore beds of culinary, medicinal, aromatic, and dye plants. Along the way, Lisa will share stories of how these herbs were cultivated and used by the Enfield Shakers, while exploring the ecology, botany, and practical uses of the plants growing in the garden today.

A lifelong science educator with a background in environmental chemistry and ecology, Lisa brings curiosity, enthusiasm, and a love of learning to every tour. After a 31-year career teaching science at Lebanon High School, she joined the Museum as an Interpreter and educator, where she enjoys helping visitors discover the rich connections between plants, history, and the Shaker way of life.

The Museum’s herb garden features many of the same plants that were grown by the Shakers as part of their thriving herb and medicine enterprise.

Saturdays at Noon.

Tours are free with Museum admission and are open to visitors of all ages. Whether you’re an avid gardener, curious about herbal traditions, or simply looking for a beautiful way to experience the Museum grounds, this tour offers a unique opportunity to explore the living legacy of the Enfield Shakers.

What to Expect

Tours last approximately one hour and take place rain or shine, except in the case of thunder or lightning. Much of the tour is outdoors in full sun, so we recommend dressing for the weather, wearing comfortable walking shoes, and bringing water, sunscreen, or rain gear as needed.

The herb garden features maintained paths, but visitors should expect some uneven terrain. Benches are available in both sunny and shaded areas throughout the garden for those who would like to sit during the tour.

Visitors are encouraged to engage all of their senses. You’ll have opportunities to see, smell, and ~when invited by your guide~ even taste selected herbs. To help preserve the garden and support the Museum’s educational mission, we ask that visitors do not pick plants or harvest herbs during the tour.

1 pm - 3 pm 107 Days at Sea: The Journey That Changed Everything Auditorium E, Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center One Medical Center Drive, Lebanon, NH 03766

At 63, Jill Chalsty boarded a ship alone, grieving her husband’s death and battling cancer. What began as a voyage around the world became far more than a trip. In this lecture, Jill shares the story behind her memoir Packets of Hope, inviting participants to travel alongside her through the ports she visited, the people she met, and the reflections that transformed personal adversity into strength and global impact. Jill demonstrates how one person’s courage can create ripples that span continents.

Participants are encouraged to read her memoir, available free at www.packetsofhope.com, before the presentation.

Jill Siegal Chalsty has devoted her life to the transformative power of education. As founder of Overcoming Obstacles, the nonprofit she launched in 1992, Jill pioneered life skills instruction that has now reached more than 180 million students worldwide. What began as a mission to help young people navigate life’s challenges has evolved into a global movement for youth empowerment. Following the profound loss of her husband and her own battles with cancer, Jill embarked on a voyage of healing and reflection. That journey inspired her memoir, Packets of Hope, an exploration of resilience, love, and finding meaning through service. She's made her book available for free at packetsofhope.com.

7:00 pm - 9:30 pm National Theatre in HD: The Misanthrope Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Sandra Oh stars in this razor-sharp reimagining of Molière's classic dark comedy.

Alice (Sandra Oh), a brilliant novelist, despises the hollow contemporary mantras of kindness and respect. But the bolder she becomes in speaking out, the more colleagues avoid her, and the more her personal relationships begin to fracture. As she challenges fashionable ideas and lends her voice to causes others are afraid to touch, she faces intense criticism and backlash. Alice will soon learn the price she must pay as an artist and as a woman for daring to speak her mind.  

First performed on 15 June 1666 at the Théâtre du Palais‑Royal in Paris, The Misanthrope emerged at a pivotal moment in the reign of Louis XIV, when court life, power and social conventions weighed heavily on the public conscience. In this context, Molière crafted a verse comedy as serious as it is brilliant, questioning the role of sincerity in a world ruled by appearances. Less farcical than his other plays, it stands as a masterpiece of balance between social satire and emotional tension—and this new production shows these moral dilemmas are utterly timeless.

2 pm - 3 pm The Power of Music: The Role Music Can Play in Alzheimer's Disease and Dementia Osher at Dartmouth 1 Court St. Lebanon, NH 03766

In partnership with the Upper Valley Walk to End Alzheimer's, Osher at Dartmouth is offering this special lecture! Discover the powerful role music can play in the lives of people living with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. This presentation explores how music can help access memories, reduce anxiety, improve communication, and foster meaningful moments of connection. We'll also discuss practical ways caregivers can use music to support their loved ones while caring for their own well-being. Whether you're a family caregiver, healthcare professional, or simply interested in the healing power of music, you'll leave with a deeper understanding of how music can bring comfort, joy, and connection throughout the dementia journey.

Allison W. Pollard, MT-BC, is a classically trained soprano, music educator, and board-certified music therapist. A native of the Upper Valley, she studied voice and music education at Miami University (Ohio) and performed with professional choirs throughout the Cincinnati area, including solo appearances in oratorio works and operatic and musical theatre productions such as Leonard Bernstein’s MASS with the Cincinnati May Festival. She also served as Director of the Children’s Chorus with Opera North, where she led young singers in mainstage productions of Carmen and The Little Prince.

Allison holds a Master of Arts in Clinical Mental Health Counseling and Music Therapy from Lesley University. She has taught music both in the United States and abroad, including teaching English through the arts in Italy, and spent five years teaching in public schools as an elementary music educator. She now teaches at the Upper Valley Music Center and, newly board-certified in music therapy, is excited to share her love of music through both performance and therapeutic practice in her home community.

5 pm - 6 pm A Student Stands: From Tiananmen to Today Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

Today China stands at odds with the United States more than ever. This is far from the enthusiastic welcome China received into the world order in 2001. Globalization of trade did not result in the liberalization in China many had assumed was inevitable. Before the Western world attempted to liberalize China from the outside, there were efforts from within. Our esteemed speaker, Mr. Zhou Fengsuo, is one such voice of dissent. In 1989, he was a physics student at Tsinghua University when he became one of the leading organizers of the Tiananmen Square protests.

The event will be livestreamed and recorded. Open and free to the public, but tickets are required. 

Livestream registration (webinar): here | In-person tickets: here

Zhou Fengsuo (born 1967 in Xi'an, China) was a physics student at Tsinghua University when he became one of the leading organizers of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. He served on the Standing Committee of the Beijing Students’ Autonomous Union, founded the protests’ official radio station “The Voice of the Student Movement,” and coordinated medical assistance for hunger-striking protesters. After the crackdown, he was listed number five on the government's most-wanted list and was forced into exile in the United States. He has spent the decades since as a tireless advocate for democracy in China. He currently serves as Executive Director of Human Rights in China, and his recent work focuses on combating the Chinese Communist Party's use of AI and digital surveillance tools to suppress dissent.

Made possible by the Davidson Institute for Global Security at Dartmouth and the Alexander Hamilton Society

2:30 pm - 3:30 pm Quantum Nano Seminar - Dr. Kourosh Shirkoohi, INRS, Québec academic Wilder Hall 115 and Zoom

Abstract: 

In cuprates — copper-oxide materials that host the highest superconducting transition temperatures at ambient pressure—even the non-superconducting state presents puzzles that have remained unresolved for decades. On the overdoped side, where the hole concentration exceeds that giving the highest superconducting transition temperature and superconductivity fades, the resistivity exhibits a prominent contribution proportional to temperature. This anomalous T-linear contribution persists towards low temperature when superconductivity is suppressed, over an extended doping range. It contrasts with the low-temperature T² contribution expected from electron–electron scattering in a conventional Fermi liquid. T-linearity is often associated with a scattering rate of Planckian order, 1/τ ∼ kBT/ℏ, where τ is the electronic relaxation time. Strange metallic behaviour is also ubiquitous across the iron-based superconductors, heavy-fermion compounds, and moiré materials such as twisted graphene, raising the possibility of a shared origin for their unconventional behaviour.

Electrical transport experiments measure the voltage response to an applied current: the longitudinal response gives the resistivity, while the transverse response in an applied magnetic field gives the Hall effect. In a simple single-carrier Drude picture, the Hall coefficient yields the carrier density, n, while the Drude resistivity, ρ = m*Γ/(ne²), combines how rapidly current relaxes through scattering (Γ), how many carriers contribute (n), and their effective mass (m*). Whether this interpretation holds in a strange metal is a central question. In overdoped cuprates, spectroscopic probes that image the Fermi surface—the boundary between occupied and unoccupied electronic states in momentum space—reveal that it remains connected and large, with a volume corresponding to n = 1 + p holes per copper site, where p is the doped-hole concentration. Yet the carrier number inferred from the Hall effect evolves strongly with doping, from approximately n = p to n = 1 + p, while the coefficient of temperature-linear resistivity, Aρ, decreases. What microscopic change drives this evolution?

We use two complementary spectroscopic probes: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which measures the energies and emission angles of electrons ejected by light, mapping the electronic spectrum as a function of energy and momentum; and Electronic Raman scattering (ERS), which measures the energy exchanged between light and electronic excitations, with light polarization weighting different regions of momentum space. Together, these probes allow us to distinguish changes in low-energy spectral weight — the strength of electronic excitations — from changes in their scattering rates, with complementary momentum sensitivity across a range of dopings spanning this enigmatic phase....

To be continued. For full abstract please contact samantha.j.marcotte@dartmouth.edu

Hosted by: Assistant Professor Rufus Boyack

2:30 pm - 3:30 pm Space and Plasma Seminar - Luca Orusa, PhD, Columbia University academic Wilder 202 and Zoom

Abstract:  Over the past decade, space-based experiments such as AMS-02, DAMPE, CALET, and Fermi-LAT, together with ground-based observatories including HAWC, H.E.S.S., and LHAASO, have transformed the study of Galactic cosmic rays and gamma rays into a precision science. This new observational era raises fundamental questions about the plasma processes responsible for particle acceleration, magnetic-field amplification, and cosmic-ray transport in astrophysical environments.

In this talk, I will show how kinetic plasma simulations provide a first-principles description of particle acceleration at shocks, and how laboratory astrophysics experiments can be used to reproduce and test key aspects of collisionless shock physics under controlled conditions. I will then discuss how cosmic rays modify the surrounding plasma close to their sources, driving instabilities and modifying the local magnetic and transport properties. Taken together, these plasma processes establish a direct connection between microscopic kinetic physics and the large-scale cosmic-ray and gamma-ray observables measured across the Galaxy.

Hosted by Dartmouth Postdocoral Associate Adrien Soudais

7:00pm Brewing in New Hampshire: An Informal History of Beer in the Granite State Gafney Library 14 High Street Sanbornville New Hampshire 03872

Glenn Knoblock explores the fascinating history of New Hampshire's beer and ale brewing industry from Colonial days, when it was home- and tavern-based, to today's modern breweries and brew pubs. Unusual and rare photos and advertisements document this changing industry and the state's earliest brewers, including the renowned Frank Jones. A number of lesser-known brewers and breweries that operated in the state are also discussed, including the only brewery owned and operated by a woman before the modern era. Illustrations present evidence of society's changing attitudes towards beer and alcohol consumption over the years. Whether you're a beer connoisseur or a "tea-totaler", this lecture will be enjoyed by adults of all ages.

This program will be held in the Community Room of the Gafney Library, located on the lower level. There is an elevator and stairs available. Free parking is across the street. No registration is required and there will be a social time after the program with snacks.

8:30 pm - 11:00 pm Metropolis (DFS: Myths Revisited) Rollins Chapel

Fritz Lang's crown jewel of silent cinema fuses the frenetic storytelling of 1920s pulp fiction with his fascination with the darker side of human nature.

Set in the year 2026, society has been divided into two rigid groups: one of rich planners or thinkers, who live in luxury on the surface of Earth in the lush skyscrapers; the other of workers, who live underground, toiling to sustain the lives of the privileged up above. Both halves are ignorant of each other. It is only when Freder Fredersen, the son of the rich city master, meets the saintly Maria from below, that he descends and sees the lives and machines that keep his society afloat. 

Determined to be the "Mediator" that Maria prophesizes to the workers, Freder must fight against lies and deception to unite the "head" of his world with the "hands" down below. Full of Biblical references and religious allegory, Metropolis fixed for the rest of the century the image of a futuristic city as a hell of scientific progress and human despair, and inspired countless narratives from Star Wars to Blade Runner. 

With live organ accompaniment by Peter Krasinski

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited." Programmed in collaboration with the William Jewett Tucker Center for Spiritual, the Department of Film & Media Studies and Ethical Living, the Church of Christ at Dartmouth College

 

This event is free and unticketed.

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm Droughts and Our Forests across the North Country TBD

A Conversation with Climatologist Lesley-Ann L. Dupigny-Giroux

The historic North Country flash droughts of 2025 and the ecological droughts of 2012 and 2016 served as a wake-up call for an improved understanding of the interplay between moisture extremes and forest health across Vermont and New Hampshire.

Dr. Lesley-Ann L. Dupigny-Giroux is a professor of climatology in UVM's Department of Geography and Geosciences, the Vermont state climatologist since 1997, and the president of the American Association of State Climatologists from 2020-2022. An applied climatologist by training, Dr. Dupigny-Giroux's research interests intersect a number of interdisciplinary fields including hydroclimatic natural hazards and climate literacy, climate services, geospatial climate and land-surface processes, all within the context of our changing climate. 

​This event is part of the Montgomery Fellows Program's Climate Solutions: Wishful Thinking or Hopeful Planning? series.

4:30 pm - 5:45 pm "Seeing Animals" Talk by photojournalist Jo-Anne McArthur audience: Alumni, Faculty, Postdoc, Staff, Students-Graduate, Students-Undergraduate Room 003, Rockefeller Center

The Anthropocene Working Group invites you to attend a talk by animal photojournalist Jo-Anne McArthur.

"Seeing Animals: The Evolving Role of Animal Photojournalism in Advocacy & Culture Change"

Wednesday, October 14, 4:30-5:45 pm, Rockefeller Center 003

Acclaimed photojournalist and founder of We Animals, Jo-Anne McArthur, explores the emerging field of Animal Photojournalism (APJ), a discipline that documents the lives of animals living in the human environment to capture both their sentience and their suffering. Drawing from We Animals' extensive field reporting, including stories on the Australian bushfires and the ground-breaking collective project HIDDEN: Animals in the Anthropocene, McArthur presents a visual journey, and offers a deep dive into how we see, and fail to see, animals through photography. The presentation examines how trying to see the world from an animal’s perspective can foster interspecies empathy. It also addresses the broader systemic realities of industrial agriculture, deforestation, and climate-induced disasters, such as the U.S. floods that have caused mass casualties of farmed animals.

Moving beyond traditional wildlife photography, and the use of animals as models, this talk critically unpacks what sets APJ apart, assessing its strategic potential for driving real-world impact alongside its ethical and practical limitations. McArthur will address how documenting animal exploitation intersects directly with critical human and environmental crises, offering a nuanced look at the evolution of this field and its role in modern journalism. The presentation will be followed by an open Q&A session.

Jo-Anne is an award-winning photojournalist, sought-after speaker, photo editor, and the founder of We Animals. She has visited over sixty countries to document our fraught relationship with animals and is the author of three books: We Animals (2014), Captive (2017), and HIDDEN: Animals in the Anthropocene (2020). Jo-Anne is the subject of the acclaimed Canadian documentary, The Ghosts in Our Machine, and her photographs have received accolades from Wildlife Photographer of the Year, Nature Photographer of the Year, Big Picture, Picture of the Year International, the Global Peace Award, and others. Jo-Anne enjoys jurying photo competitions and has done so for World Press Photo, Big Picture, and others. She hails from Toronto, Canada.

6:00pm Corbin’s Animal Garden Walpole Town Library 48 Main Street Walpole NH 03608

In the late 1800s, the banking, railroad, and real estate mogul Austin Corbin returned to his hometown in Newport, New Hampshire. He built a grand estate and bought out his neighbors’ farms to create an 22,000 acre wildlife game preserve stocked with boar, bison, bighorn sheep, antelope, elk, Chinese pheasant, and other imported animals. The grounds eventually became a prestigious private hunting park and hosted illustrious guests including Theodore Roosevelt, the Prince of Wales, Cornelius Vanderbilt, Joe DiMaggio, Rudyard Kipling, and Augustus Saint-Gaudens.

This illustrated slideshow features archival images and a discussion of the complicated history and legacy of New Hampshire’s own American Gilded Age robber baron. The talk will also highlight the important legacy of the role the Corbin family and park naturalist Ernest Baynes played in the saving of the American bison from extinction.

Pre-registration is recommended. To register, call 603-756-9806 or email  jmalmberg@walpoletownlibrary.org.

12:15 pm - 1:00 pm Research Talk – Chris Sollars: The Neighbors 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center

Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies Joseph Tumber-Dávila is a terrestrial ecosystems ecologist studying the response of ecosystems to global environmental change. Joseph's research program as an ecologist investigates global environmental change effects on terrestrial ecosystems, plant functional traits, and subsequent consequences for global carbon cycling and policy. As a terrestrial ecosystem ecologist, Joseph's unique, interdisciplinary, approach spans regional and global scale experiments, syntheses, and modeling. 

Assistant Professor of Geography Arianna M Varuolo-Clarke, is interested in understanding how the distribution of water around the globe will change. Her research questions center around three main questions. First, how does anthropogenic forcing influence past hydroclimate variability and change? Second, how does natural (internal) climate variability influence hydroclimate variability and change? Third, what is the combined influence of anthropogenic forcings impact on natural climate variability on hydroclimate variability and change? I seek to use observations and climate models to better understand the relative drivers of past hydroclimate change so that we can better constrain our projections of future water availability.

Together Assistant Professor Joseph Tumber-Dávila and Assistant Professor of Geography Arianna M Varuolo-Clarke are using high resolution climate model simulations and forest models to quantify the impact of future hurricane impact on forest carbon storage in New England.

This programming accompanies a faculty exhibition by Associate Professor of Studio Art Chris Sollars, The Neighbors, a new body of work inspired by coexistence and inquiry.

Set in rural Vermont, The Neighbors is a multimedia video installation about the non-human inhabitants of the lands around the artist’s home. After over two decades living in San Francisco, California, Sollars moved to Vermont in the fall of 2024. To get to know his new home and neighbors, he has spent the past two years interacting with his surroundings through slow listening and observation, learning them spatially and temporally.  This intentional gathering of information has taken the form of diaristic snapshots taken throughout the seasons, field recordings, the collection of discarded nests and materials, and the placement of wildlife cameras in the open woodland edges of his home, which neighbors a land trust, a national forest, and the Appalachian Trail.

The Neighbors is on view from Sept. 15 – Nov. 8, 2026.

Humanities Is a Team Sport
If you think the humanities are a solo practice, think again. The future will be built on teams, partnerships, and coalitions.

Free & Open to All

Elizabeth Greene, University of Western Ontario

Talk title: Archaeological Leather and the Precarious Future of Organic Material Evidence

Abstract: The Roman site of Vindolanda on the northern frontier of Britain has provided one of the best assemblages of organic material from anywhere in the empire. Over eight thousand leather finds, including nearly five thousand shoes, and countless wood and bone objects, have provided a more complete picture of life in the past than is typical of most sites. However, this invaluable resource is also under threat from environmental shifts, and Vindolanda is leading the way on several initiatives to understand how climate change is affecting archaeological remains. This talk will first present current work on archaeological leather and then focus on its role in assessing the impact of climate change on archaeology and organic artifacts.

Generously funded by Gino Franco Luigi Zarbin, MD Memorial Fund in Classics.

4:30 pm - 6:30 pm Saints and Silks: The global reach of Latin Christianity in the Middle Ages Carson Hall L02

Julia Smith, Emeritus Chichele Professor of Medieval History, All Souls College
Oxford University

Thursday, October 15, 2026
4:30 PM
Location: Carson L02
Free and open to all

Reception to follow

Lecture title: Saints and Silks: The global reach of Latin Christianity in the early Middle Ages

Abstract: This illustrated lecture uses the contents of Christian reliquaries from the first half of the European Middle Ages to reflect on how relics accumulated in medieval churches and how their textile wrappers enhanced their sacred aura.  In so doing, it offers a focussed way of thinking through some of the implications of the global turn for study of medieval Europe.  Utilising textual sources such as relic labels and inventories on the one hand and, on the other, material evidence, especially textiles, it takes an ‘object biography’ approach to emphasise the rich complexity of ecclesiastical relic collections.  While the examples chosen will span Eurasia, the argument emphasises the local contexts in which relics accumulated and thus the distinctive profile of each collection.  The lecture replaces conventional textbook accounts of the early medieval West with a dynamic picture of contingency, mobility, and repurposing which sustained the religious capital of early medieval churches in the Latin West.

The James and David Orr Memorial Lectures on Culture and Religion bring to Dartmouth each year scholars and writers whose achievements are at the highest level, but whose main fields of interest are not necessarily religion. 5 pm - 6 pm Aurelian Craiutu, Moderation as Political Strategy--Past and Present Room 002, Rockefeller Center

Moderation is a contested concept that, with surprisingly few exceptions, is absent from our public debates. Today, the single famous line that people sometimes may remember belongs to Barry Goldwater: “Extremism in the pursuit of liberty is no vice, moderation in the pursuit of justice is no virtue.” His witty words continue to provoke and invite us to rethink the nature of moderation and examine its eclecticism. The latter can be explored by looking at the many faces of moderation and the various agendas and principles moderates of all types advanced over time. 

The lecture will address the following questions: What kind of virtue is political moderation and how can we study it? What does it mean to be a moderate voice in politics? What are the limits and benefits of moderation? Finally, can moderation be a winning card in our hyper-polarized political world?

Craiutu is the Arthur F. Bentley Professor and Chair of the Department of Political Science at Indiana University, Bloomington. His most recent book is Why Not Moderation? Letters to a Young Radical (Cambridge University Press, 2024). His talk is sponsored by the Political Economy Project and the Rockefeller Center.

5:00 pm - 6:30 pm Ziad Abu-Rish,"The State of Lebanon: Popular Politics and Institution Building" Kemeny Hall 008
Drawing from his recent work, The State of Lebanon, Ziad Abu-Rish traces shifting patterns of alliances and conflict that shaped the material and representational production of the Lebanese nation-state, formed in 1943. His new social and institutional history of post-colonial Lebanon challenges common narratives of Lebanon as an absent, weak, or failed state. Instead, state institutional arrangements emerge as objects and subjects of political mobilization by politicians, bureaucrats, party activists, students, and workers. His research offers significant insights into politics, social life, and the state in Lebanon—grounded in the early post-independence period yet critical to how we understand Lebanon today.

Ziad Abu-Rish is a scholar of the modern Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region at Bard College. A historian by training, his research centers around state formation, economic development, and popular mobilizations, particularly in Lebanon and Jordan. Abu-Rish is the author of The State of Lebanon: Popular Politics and Institution Building in the Wake of Independence (Stanford University Press, 2026). He co-created (with artist Tania El Khoury) The Search for Power, a touring lecture performance and sound installation exploring the history of electricity in Beirut. Abu-Rish is also coeditor of The Dawn of the Arab Uprisings: End of an Old Order? (2012) and Critical Voices: A Collection of Interviews from and on the Middle East (2015). He has also authored several articles and chapters on the political economy of the Middle East, popular protests and movements in Lebanon and Jordan, and teaching Middle East history. Abu-Rish serves as coeditor of Jadaliyya e-zine and codirector of the Lebanese Dissertation Summer Institute. His media appearances include Al Jazeeera, BBC, and Democracy Now!.

6:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution Kimball Library 5 Academy Avenue Atkinson NH 03811

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

7:00 pm - 8:15 pm Preconceived Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

A riveting documentary about the pervasive but overlooked presence of Crisis Pregnancy Centers.

Where does someone turn when facing an unplanned pregnancy? This even-handed film offers a raw and insightful look into the rise of the enigmatic crisis pregnancy centers (CPCs), many of which are a part of a movement striving to make abortion unthinkable and illegal. The documentary explores the complex role of deception, finances, faith and privacy in the CPC industry, while also showing that many of the people involved genuinely believe they are serving the greater good.

Preconceived follows the stories of two women, Maleeha in Texas and Maria in Colorado, whose searches to terminate their unplanned pregnancies misled them to anti-abortion centers. The film also features testimonies from individuals on both sides of the issue, including leaders of the CPC industry as well as experts who caution why many CPC practices are problematic. Amid a shifting legal landscape, Preconceived deftly navigates the complicated political and moral knot that is abortion access in America and underscores the importance of understanding the resources available to pregnant people.

Discussion follows. Co-hosted by the Dartmouth Democrats and the Hanover/Lyme Democrats, in collaboration with Reproductive Equity Now.
